properties.decision:
OPEN, and deliberately NOT a reopening of `dec:where-content-lives`. Anthony confirmed 2026-07-31 to proceed with the committed-blob recommendation "for now and we can reconsider when or if we do the full object_store implementation" — so this records a live pressure and the condition under which it becomes a fork again.

THE ARGUMENT, IN HIS SHARPER FORM. The first version of this note said the appeal of an external store was size relief. That undersells it. His framing: "going with an external storage allows for ALL documentation to be stored and referenced." The point is not that the repository gets smaller — it is that THE NEED TO BE SELECTIVE DISAPPEARS. `dec:content-growth-is-bounded-by-what-not-by-size` solves the measured problem by rationing: transcripts by exception, judgement exercised every time. That works, and it is a STANDING TAX ON JUDGEMENT rather than a one-off cost. An external store removes the question instead of answering it.

WHICH CHANGES WHAT WOULD REOPEN THIS. The original condition was "total grows past what a clone should reasonably carry, with the by-exception rule followed". Keep it, and add the one his framing implies: IF THE RATIONING ITSELF PROVES COSTLY — if sessions routinely spend judgement deciding what is worth keeping, or if things that should have been kept were not — then the tax is real and the fork is back, whatever the byte count says. A discipline that works only because someone is paying attention every time is a discipline with a running cost, and that cost is the thing to watch, not only the total.

WHY NOT NOW, unchanged: the policy addresses the measured problem directly, and reflow2's entire design prose is 3.5 MB. Reopening an architectural choice to solve something a policy already solves is the wrong order, and the no-service property — clone and you have everything, nothing to configure, nothing to be down — is worth more than the convenience.

WHAT IS ALREADY UNDERSTOOD, so the reopening starts from evidence rather than from scratch. `object_store` (Apache Arrow) is recorded as the documented upgrade path in `dec:content-store-implementation`, WITH ITS COST MEASURED: 36 crates new to this workspace, ~24 of them URL/ICU machinery, and an async runtime reaching a core deliberately kept synchronous. Its unified API over S3, Azure, GCS, local files and memory is exactly what makes the backend a runtime detail — and content addressing is what makes the swap safe, because a blob verifies wherever it came from. The migration is understood; only its warrant is open.

THE PROPERTY THAT WOULD BE SPENT: a second thing to configure, be down, and fall out of step — and a consumer who skips it sees a design with holes and cannot tell. `req:content-reaches-every-seat` is the requirement under pressure, not merely a preference. An answer must say what happens to the person who has the repo and not the credentials.
properties.name: OPEN — a recorded pressure on committed blobs: the real argument is not size relief, it is not having to ration
properties.rationale:
Amended rather than left, because the first version had the argument slightly wrong and a wrong argument on the record is worse than none — it would have set up the reopening as a size question when the better case is about recurring judgement cost.

Recorded at all for the reason the same day already demonstrated twice: `cap:what-next` carried its blocker in prose and nothing noticed when the condition cleared. A lean stated in passing has that shape exactly. Writing the condition down is what makes it a trigger rather than a mood.

This is the THIRD pressure on the no-service family, after `dec:central-host` and the content store itself. Three from unrelated directions is a fact about the decision worth having on the record — not an argument to change it, and not something to keep rediscovering from first principles.
